content: Coronaviruses are named for their crown-like appearance due to the projections on their surface. The first coronavirus was isolated from chickens in 1937. The novel coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, is the etiological agent responsible for COVID-19, a respiratory illness first identified in Wuhan, China. The World Health Organization (WHO) declared the COVID-19 outbreak a pandemic on March 12, 2020. SARS-CoV-2 can be classified into two major types: the L type, which accounts for approximately 70% of cases, and the S type, which accounts for about 30%. COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a novel coronavirus named for its similarity in symptoms to those caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS). Unlike SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2 can be transmitted during the prodromal period when infected individuals are mildly ill and continue their usual activities, contributing to the rapid spread of the infection. The primary pathogenesis of COVID-19 involves severe pneumonia, RNAemia, ground-glass opacities on imaging, and acute cardiac injury. Person-to-person transmission occurs mainly through direct contact or respiratory droplets expelled by coughing or sneezing from an infected individual. COVID-19 should be differentiated from other diseases presenting with symptoms such as cough, fever, shortness of breath, and tachypnea. Globally, over 952,100 cases of COVID-19 have been reported, with 48,300 deaths. In the United States, more than 200,000 cases have been reported, with 5,100 deaths. Due to rapidly evolving data, the exact incidence rate of COVID-19 cannot be determined. The disease has spread to all continents, and WHO has declared it a pandemic. Inconsistent reporting and lack of organized data have made it difficult to establish a universal case-fatality rate. Middle-aged and elderly populations are most commonly affected, with a median age of 49–56 years. Males are more frequently affected than females. The majority of cases have been reported in China, but the disease has now spread worldwide. Exposure remains the most significant risk factor for infection. Individuals at higher risk for severe disease include those aged 60 and older, patients with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, hypertension, cancer, and those in long-term care facilities. Currently, there are no recommended guidelines for routine screening for COVID-19. Screening criteria include a history of international travel, exposure to a confirmed COVID-19 case, and symptoms such as fever, cough, fatigue, and shortness of breath. In symptomatic patients, clinical features typically appear within a week and include fever, cough, nasal congestion, fatigue, and other signs of upper respiratory tract infections. Disease progression and severity are marked by dyspnea and severe chest symptoms, with pneumonia occurring in approximately 75% of patients. The WHO has published diagnostic criteria to identify patients requiring confirmation of COVID-19 through PCR or antibody detection tests. These criteria include epidemiological and clinical factors that must be met for a suspected or confirmed diagnosis. A patient’s history may include international travel to areas with high COVID-19 prevalence. Common symptoms appearing 2–14 days after exposure include fever, cough, fatigue, and shortness of breath. Physical examination findings in COVID-19 patients include fever, flu-like symptoms, cough, and body aches. The general appearance of the patient depends on the incubation period of the illness. Laboratory tests can confirm whether the illness is caused by human coronaviruses. Specific tests include serology for viral antigens, molecular testing, and viral culture. Additional markers such as troponin, lactate dehydrogenase, interleukin-4, and procalcitonin may also be evaluated. There are no specific ECG findings associated with coronavirus infection. Non-specific findings may include sinus tachycardia, ST-elevation, and diffuse T-wave inversion. Chest X-ray findings in suspected cases may mimic pneumonia. Severe cases progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) may show a characteristic white-out appearance on chest X-rays. Echocardiography and ultrasound findings specific to coronavirus infection are not identified. Non-specific findings may include left ventricular systolic dysfunction and pericardial effusion. Chest CT scans in COVID-19 patients may reveal unilateral or bilateral pneumonia, mottling, ground-glass opacities, focal or multifocal opacities, consolidation, and septal thickening, with subpleural and lower lobe involvement being more common. MRI findings specific to coronavirus infection are not identified, but MRI may assist in diagnosis by exclusion. No other imaging findings are associated with COVID-19. Research laboratories have utilized isolation methods, electron microscopy, serology, and PCR-based assays to diagnose coronavirus infections for surveillance studies. Treatment for COVID-19 includes supportive measures and symptomatic management. No specific treatment is currently available. During the influenza season, patients presenting with COVID-19 were empirically treated with oral and intravenous antibiotics and oseltamivir (75 mg twice daily). Corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 40–120 mg/day) were administered in cases of severe community-acquired pneumonia. Oxygen therapy (via nasal cannula or invasive mechanical ventilation) was provided to patients with severe hypoxemia. Surgery is not indicated in the management of COVID-19. There is currently no vaccine to prevent COVID-19. The best way to prevent infection is to avoid exposure to the virus. As a precaution against co-infection during the flu and respiratory disease season, the CDC recommends getting a flu vaccine, practicing everyday preventive actions to stop the spread of germs, and taking flu antivirals if prescribed. Healthcare providers are advised to monitor individuals who recently traveled from China and present with fever and respiratory symptoms.
